claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni FCC alloys and their quaternary and ternary subsets are primarily governed by local lattice distortion and stacking-fault energy.
Increasing the number of constituents increases atomic-size mismatch.
Greater atomic-size mismatch enhances local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion modifies stacking-fault energy.
Enhanced local lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation motion.
Enhanced local lattice distortion promotes dynamic strain aging.
Enhanced local lattice distortion promotes deformation twinning.
Dynamic strain aging and deformation twinning increase yield strength and work hardening.
Higher-constituent-count alloys have higher yield strength than lower-constituent-count subsets.
Higher-constituent-count alloys have higher work-hardening rates than lower-constituent-count subsets.
Higher-constituent-count alloys exhibit more deformation twinning than lower-constituent-count subsets.
Lower-constituent-count subsets have less lattice distortion than the quinary alloy.
Lower-constituent-count subsets have a higher effective stacking-fault energy than the quinary alloy.
Identical thermomechanical processing can produce comparable grain sizes and single-phase FCC structures across the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Controlling grain size, phase constitution, temperature, and strain rate isolates compositional effects on mechanical behavior.
The proposed mechanism is limited to comparable, single-phase FCC microstructures and may fail when multiphase behavior, major grain-size changes, or deformation-mechanism changes occur.

contradictions.description: The prediction is phrased as alloys with more constituents outperforming the five-component quinary baseline, although the defined candidate series contains only quaternary and ternary subsets with fewer constituents. The intended comparison appears to be the quinary baseline versus its lower-count subsets.
